newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Buyers bullish on Ukraine T-bill market - trade.
newsitem.headline: Buyers bullish on Ukraine T-bill market - trade.

text.p: Buyers were taking a bullish view of Ukraine's money markets in the light of recent International Monetary Fund and U.S. government decisions on funding to the former Soviet republic, traders said on Monday.

An IMF mission is visiting Kiev this week to discuss granting an interim stand-by credit in an unknown amount until Ukraine fulfils 41 conditions to qualify for a three-year, $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility.

The U.S. government last week allocated $225 million to Ukraine, the third largest recipient of U.S. foreign aid after Egypt, but said only half would be released until Washington confirmed progress on reforms and the fight against corruption.

"In general things are fairly bullish for Ukraine at the moment, given the stand-by and the U.S. aid," said David Atkinson, a strategist with Deutche Morgan Grenfell's local currency proprietary trading division in London.
"The consensus is that things look positive for the hryvnia," he added.
The hryvnia was unchanged at 1.8570 to the dollar on the Ukrainian Interbank Currency Exchange on Monday. The authorities have been holding the hryvnia in a 1.70-1.90 trading band since 1995.
Average yields at Treasury bill auctions last Thursday slipped to 20.15 percent from 20.17 percent for six-month bills and to 27.71 from 27.73 percent for nine-month bills.
Twelve-month bills dipped to 29.99 from 30.04 percent, and 18-month paper was unchanged at 32.53 percent.
Wood and Company senior analyst Patricia Bartholomew said there may be a further slight drop in yields, reflecting a general trend since the beginning of the year.
"It should continue on that trend," she said. "It should be the same as for most weeks."
Bartholomew said the hryvnia would likely remain at 1.8570 to the dollar, its rate since mid-June.
But Igor Frunze, a trade with Finance and Credit Invest bank, said the start of summer holidays meant markets would be quiet with prices little changed.
"It will be the usual. It's summer," Frunze said.
